newsitem.title: USA: U.S. offers money laundering rules for non-banks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. offers money laundering rules for non-banks.

text.p: With illicit money laundering moving from highly-regulated banks to local check cashing outlets and money remitters, U.S. Treasury Department proposed on Monday new reporting rules for non-bank transactions.

Money laundering is the "life blood of organized crime," Treasury Secretary Rubin said at a news briefing here. "But it is also the 'Achilles heel,' as it gives us a way to attack the leaders of criminal organizations."
Under the proposal, money remitters will have to report all transfers of more than $750 out of the United States.
Such money remitters transfer about $11 billion a year, both within and outside of the country, usually in amounts of less than $500, Treasury officials said.
A broader array of money service businesses, including firms that issue money orders or travellers checks, will have to register with the government and report suspicious activity as banks do now.
Under Secretary of Enforcement Raymond Kelly said the new $750 reporting requirement was based on a successful program in the New York City area known as Operation El Dorado.

"We estimated that 12 transmitters in Queens county alone sent $800 million to Colombia each year," Kelly told reporters. "To account for this money legitimately, each Colombian household in the area would have had to wire $30,000, an amount which exceeds the average annual income in this community by $3,000."
So federal officials required the transmitter to report all transfer to Colombia over $750.
"The results were immediate and dramatic," Kelly said. Money launders were forced to smuggle cash out of the city, leading to seizures of $50 million in eastern ports, he said.

The new rules will not generate a substantial increase in the volume of reports already handled by the government, according to Stanley Morris, director or the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network known as FinCEN.
The Internal Revenue Service collects about 12 million reports a year from banks and other firms, Morris said.
"That 12 million of currency reports includes all banks in the United States, so this is a small increment -- certainly less than a million," Morris said.

The rules "are needed and they make sense," Rep. Henry Gonzalez, Deomocrat of Texas, said in a statement. "The lesson learned from the Texas border experience is that strong but reasonable regulatory oversight of a vulnerable financial segment can go a long way in interrupting, and shutting down, a money laundering pipeline."
The proposal was issued for comment for 90 days and should be enacted in final form by the end of the year, Kelly said.
